extracted.intended_audience: marketers, advertisers, brand managers, and advertising researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for using humor in advertising, grounded in Benign Violation Theory; intended to help creatives and marketers decide when humor will help versus hurt a campaign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the violation clearly benign for the target audience?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the humorous violation is perceived as benign rather than aversive by the intended audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benign appraisal mediates humor effectiveness. If the violation is ambiguous or likely to be seen as aversive, humor will fail. Use audience testing to confirm benign interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the butt of the joke distant from the audience?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the joke's target is socially/cognitively distant from the ad's audience (friends/ingroup vs. outgroup/competitor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distance reduces alienation — jokes aimed at distant or symbolic targets are less likely to offend affiliates. Avoid targeting groups closely tied to your audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does humor distract from or enhance the product message?
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether humorous elements help communicate the product benefit or merely generate laughter that obscures product information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure whether message recall and persuasion metrics improve. Anti-pattern: humor that dominates attention but leaves viewers unclear on the product or offer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is aggression dialed appropriately (low > high)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge the level of aggressive humor used — low-aggressive tends to promote engagement, while high-aggressive can backfire once a threshold is crossed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer low-aggressive humor for broad audiences; reserve higher aggression only when other safeguards (e.g., audience distance, competitor target) exist and test for backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Could a reasonable consumer be offended?
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate whether an average consumer would find the ad offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is plausible offense, reconsider or rework. Offensive ads can reduce purchase intent even if they are funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the product familiar and a low-stakes use case?
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the product category is familiar and the usage scenario is low-risk for consumers — contexts where humor performs better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor is more effective for familiar, low-stakes products; for unfamiliar or high-stakes products, prioritize clarity and trust-building over humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the target audience already favorably disposed?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess baseline audience sentiment toward the brand before deploying humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor works best when audiences are already favorable; attempting edgy humor with hostile or neutral audiences increases risk of negative outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid highly inappropriate (aversive) humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use humor that constitutes an aversive violation — content that elicits disgust, strong moral outrage, or severe offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aversive violations prompt avoidance (disgust + laughter) and reduce persuasive outcomes. Screen creative for potential moral/ethical triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid humor with a specific target/butt that alienates the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid jokes that single out specific groups or individuals closely connected to the audience unless the target is a rival brand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific-target humor risks alienating the targeted group's affiliates. Exception: brand-to-brand teasing where competitors are socially acceptable targets for mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid humor that prompts avoidance (disgust + laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use humor that causes simultaneous disgust and amusement, which leads viewers to avoid the ad or brand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such reactions lower persuasion and can harm brand perception. Use pretesting to detect simultaneous negative-affect reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funniness does not equal persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that an ad being funny does not guarantee it will persuade or increase purchase intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both entertainment (funniness) and outcome measures (brand recall, attitude change, purchase intent); optimize for persuasive outcomes, not just laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance from violation matters; too aggressive can alienate target's affiliates
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for social distance between the audience and the violation: greater proximity increases risk that affiliates will feel implicated and react negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aggression is used, ensure target is sufficiently distant (e.g., competitor brands) or risk alienating those connected to the target; consider segment-specific reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand-to-brand teasing: aggressive humor may be benign when targeting competitors
rubrics_metrics.description: When the target is a rival brand, aggressive humor can be perceived as benign and accepted by many consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brand-to-brand teasing can work, but still test for overreach. Monitor for escalation effects and potential negative spillover to your brand among neutral or competitor-affiliated audiences.
